features.title: APScheduler background jobs — Teller sync, balance reconciliation, profile refresh
features.description: APScheduler is wired into the FastAPI lifespan with 6 jobs: (1) coach_morning: morning digest 07:00 daily; (2) coach_evening: evening digest 17:30 daily; (3) coach_weekly: weekly digest Fri 17:00; (4) profile_scheduled_refresh: profile refresh Sun 03:00; (5) teller_background_sync: transaction sync */4h:30 — pulls new posted transactions for all linked accounts without calling the balance API; (6) teller_balance_sync: weekly balance anchor Mon 04:00 — fetches live Teller balance, stores balance_at_last_sync + balance_synced_at on budget_accounts, resets current_balance. Between weekly syncs, current_balance = balance_at_last_sync + SUM(transactions since balance_synced_at), keeping displayed balance accurate without per-sync API calls. Silent weekly reconciliation corrects drift. Cost: ~4 balance API calls/account/month ($0.40) vs daily ($3.00).

features.title: Category groups — collapsible category sections
features.description:
Allow budget categories to be organized into named groups. Groups are collapsible in the UI. Each category belongs to one group; ungrouped categories fall into a default 'Other' bucket. Requires a new budget_category_groups table with a sort_order and name, and a group_id FK on budget_categories. The /budget/categories response should nest categories inside their group. On first setup, seed the default groups and assignments listed below.

Proposed default groups (inspired by YNAB, adapted for Hearth):

Group 1 — Fixed Monthly (sort 1): Immediate recurring obligations, roughly the same every month. Default categories: Housing, Utilities, Insurance, Subscriptions.

Group 2 — Everyday Spending (sort 2): Regular variable spending that happens most weeks. Default categories: Groceries, Dining, Transportation, Personal Care.

Group 3 — Irregular / True Expenses (sort 3): Predictable but infrequent — plan for these monthly even when they do not hit every month (the YNAB true-expenses concept). Default categories: Household, Healthcare, Travel, Gifts, Education, Shopping.

Group 4 — Savings & Goals (sort 4): Money leaving the spending pool for a future purpose. Default categories: Savings.

Group 5 — Just for Fun (sort 5): Discretionary and lifestyle spending. Default categories: Entertainment, Gaming, Vices.

Group 6 — Income (sort 6): Inflows; displayed separately from spending groups. Default categories: Income.

features.title: Workout data model refactor — first-class sets, exercise library, superset groups
features.description:
Foundation for all subsequent workout features. The existing model likely stores sets as JSONB on the exercise row; this refactor promotes sets to first-class rows and introduces an exercise library. Audit the current workout domain (api/src/life_dashboard/domains/workouts/) before starting — preserve any passing behaviour.

Target schema:
- exercises: id, name, muscle_groups[] (JSONB), equipment_type, tracking_type ('reps'|'duration'|'distance'), is_global (bool — pre-seeded library entries), created_by_user_id (nullable for global). Seed ~60 common exercises on migration.
- workout_templates: id, user_id, name, description, estimated_duration_minutes, last_used_at (nullable timestamp).
- template_exercises: id, template_id, exercise_id, position (int), superset_group_id (nullable UUID — same UUID = same superset, max 5 exercises per group), default_sets (int), default_reps (nullable int), default_weight (nullable decimal), default_rest_seconds (nullable int), notes (nullable text).
- workout_sessions: id, user_id, template_id (nullable FK), name, started_at, ended_at (nullable), notes (nullable).
- session_exercises: id, session_id, exercise_id, template_exercise_id (nullable FK for pre-load), position (int), superset_group_id (nullable UUID), notes (nullable).
- workout_sets: id, session_exercise_id, set_number (int), reps (nullable int), target_reps (nullable int — planned reps, for detecting failures), duration_seconds (nullable int — for timed exercises), weight (nullable decimal), weight_unit ('lbs'|'kg'), distance_meters (nullable decimal — for cardio exercises like running/cycling/rowing), distance_unit ('km'|'mi', nullable), rest_seconds (nullable int), is_warmup (bool default false), rpe (nullable int 1–10), completed_at (nullable timestamp).

User settings: add prompt_save_as_template boolean (default true) to control the post-session save prompt.

Superset rules enforced at the service layer: a superset_group_id must have 2–5 members within the same template or session; attempting to add a 6th returns 400. When an exercise is removed from a group that would leave only 1 member, clear superset_group_id from the remaining member too.

UPDATE (2026-07-20) — scoping decision, supersedes the user_id keying above:

WORKOUTS ARE PERSONAL, TEMPLATES AND EXERCISES ARE SHARED. Sessions belong to
one member and are never shown to other members; there is deliberately NO
per-workout visibility control in the UI — that complexity is not wanted.
Sharing happens socially (showing someone your screen), not through the app.

But 'personal' is a UI decision, not a schema one. Every table keeps
household_id, so household deletion cascades cleanly, exports and backups stay
household-shaped, and the audit log and agent surface keep their scoping. The
personal-ness is enforced by always filtering on the owner, not by omitting the
column. Concretely, replacing the user_id keying above:

- exercises: add household_id, NULLABLE. NULL = app-wide seeded library
  (is_global=true, the ~60 rows). NON-NULL = a custom exercise created in that
  household, visible to its members and no one else.
- workout_templates: household_id NOT NULL + created_by_user_id. Shared with
  the whole household — a parent can build a template their kid starts from.
- workout_sessions: household_id NOT NULL + created_by_user_id (the owner).
  Personal: every read filters created_by_user_id = current user.
- workout_sessions.template_id: nullable FK, ON DELETE SET NULL. Deleting a
  template must not destroy anyone's logs — sessions materialize their own
  session_exercises and workout_sets at start, so past history survives intact
  and only future prefill is affected. Same for
  session_exercises.template_exercise_id.

DROP last_used_at from workout_templates. With shared templates it is ambiguous
(last used by whom?) and a cached column would go stale. Derive it per user
instead: MAX(started_at) FROM workout_sessions WHERE template_id = :t AND
created_by_user_id = :me. Same for exercise recency, which workouts-002 sorts by
but which was never given a column on exercises at all.

features.title: Budget profiles — scope/profile separation (data model cleanup)
features.description:
Cleanly decouple 'scope' (visibility within a profile) from 'profile' (financial context/attribution). Currently the scope column on transactions conflates both concepts. After profiles exist, scope should mean only: is this transaction private to the owner, or shared with all profile members? Attribution is handled by profile_id (via the account).

Migration: for existing transactions, scope='household' → scope='shared' + profile=Household profile; scope='personal' → scope='private' + profile=Personal profile. Rename scope enum values from 'personal'/'household' to 'private'/'shared' to remove the naming ambiguity. Update all service layer queries, schemas, and frontend references accordingly.

Verify household-scoped transactions (now scope='shared') are visible to all profile members

features.title: Budget profiles — cross-profile transaction re-attribution
features.description: Handle the common case where a transaction imported into one profile actually belongs in another (e.g. Alice pays a shared grocery run on her personal card, but the expense belongs in the Household profile). Add a nullable profile_id override column to budget_transactions. When set, it overrides the account's profile for analytics, categorization, and visibility — the transaction physically stays linked to its account (for balance tracking) but analytically lives in the target profile.

Category groups are pre-seeded for a business context: Revenue, Cost of Goods, Operating Expenses, Owner's Pay.

Account balances returned by Teller overwrite the manual current_balance field (budget-017) when a sync runs.

features.title: User profile + bootstrap pass (Phase 1 of AI coach redesign)
features.description: A persistent, per-user markdown profile that captures who the user is — current focuses, values, recurring patterns, what drains/works, things to not bring up. Stored on the existing member_ai_memory.memory_text column (reused rather than introducing a new user_profiles table — the chatbot was already reading it). The new bits: (1) last_bootstrapped_at column on member_ai_memory so we can tell whether the richer bootstrap pass has run; (2) a new user_profile_updates table holding proposed AI changes that the user accepts or rejects — the AI never silently rewrites the profile via this surface. (3) A bootstrap pass (POST /ai/profile/bootstrap) reads the user's notes, documents, active goals/projects/habits, and the last 90 days of completed todos to draft an initial profile. (4) The coach now loads the profile into its system prompt alongside the existing behavioral context; the chatbot already read memory_text so it benefits automatically. (5) A new 'Profile' subsection in Settings → AI: view current profile, edit directly, run bootstrap, review/accept/reject pending proposals. See docs/ai-coach-redesign.md for the full design.

features.title: Notes-driven incremental profile proposer (Phase 1.5 of AI coach redesign)
features.description: Closes the 'profile goes stale between bootstrap clicks' gap. After every N net-new notes (default 5) created or updated by a user, a background task runs the same proposer prompt as bootstrap but with a smaller, fresher source bundle (the last 15 notes). It either creates a pending UserProfileUpdate (source='incremental') or returns SKIP silently — the system prompt biases hard toward SKIP. Counter `notes_at_last_proposal` lives on member_ai_memory and advances even when the proposer skips, so each user can never trigger more than one proposer call per N new notes. Skips entirely until bootstrap has run at least once.

Run bootstrap and accept the proposal; profile is now populated
Create 4 new notes; verify NO proposer call yet (under threshold)

Accept the incremental proposal; verify memory_text is replaced and last_updated_at advances
Verify a note write that fails the proposer call (e.g. AI provider misconfigured) does NOT block the note save — the note commit completes, errors are logged

features.title: Journal signal extraction (Phase 2 of AI coach redesign)
features.description: Per-entry structured signal extraction for journal notes. Adds a 'kind' column to collections (kind='journal' identifies journal collections). When a note in a journal-kind collection is saved AND the user has ai_journal_extraction_enabled=true AND a provider is configured, a background asyncio task extracts {sentiment in [-1,+1], self_talk_valence (positive/neutral/harsh/mixed), themes[], notable_phrases[], energy_level, entry_date, extraction_version} and upserts a journal_signals row keyed by note_id. Coach trend helpers (sentiment_trend, harsh_self_talk_streak, dominant_themes_recent) live in journal_signal_service for Phase 3 to use.

features.title: CBT-aware coach prompt rewrite (Phase 3 of AI coach redesign)
features.description: Coach prompts rewritten to reason across all three context layers (profile, narrative signals, raw recent entries) plus existing behavioral data. New _fetch_narrative_context helper pulls sentiment trend, harsh-self-talk streak, dominant themes, and the last 5 journal entries verbatim. New _COACH_METHOD_PROMPT system-prompt fragment defines the CBT moves: reality-test harsh self-talk against strong-week data, be honest (not flattering) during real dips, 'bird by bird' register during double-negatives, no manufactured lessons during double-positives, no name-dropping the profile, journal quoting capped at one per response.

Inspect the assembled system prompt — verify order: tone voice → '## How to coach' → method prompt → profile fragment
Inspect the user message — verify it contains a '## Recent narrative' section with sentiment numbers, themes, and recent journal entries

Verify the coach never name-drops the profile across 10 sample runs

features.title: Silent profile + auto-bootstrap on API key save + key validation
features.description: Three connected UX changes that turn the AI profile from a user-facing surface into a quiet background service. features.title: Profile versioning + weekly scheduled refresh + decay (Phase 4)

The saved content appends to today's existing journal entry.

features.title: Workout template builder UX — exercise library, superset linking, drag-to-reorder
features.description:
The template editing interface where users pre-build workouts before arriving at the gym. Requires workouts-001 (data model) to be complete first.

Exercise list in a template:
- Each exercise row shows: 3-dot handle | exercise name | target sets summary | → (tap to drill into detail).
- Standalone exercises and collapsed superset rows are both first-class items in the list.
- A collapsed superset row renders as 'Exercise A + Exercise B' (or 'Exercise A + 2 others' for 3+). It has one 3-dot handle, one tap target, and counts as one draggable item.

3-dot handle behaviour:
- Single tap: opens a context menu containing: Edit exercise settings, Link as superset, Unlink superset (only when in a superset), Add note, Remove exercise.
- Tap-and-hold: activates drag-to-reorder for that row. Dragging a collapsed superset row moves the entire group as a unit.

Superset link mode (entered via 3-dot → 'Link as superset'):
- All 3-dot icons become checkboxes. The tapped exercise is pre-checked.
- User taps additional exercises (standalone or collapsed supersets) to select them.
- Fixed bottom bar shows [Cancel] and [Link] (disabled until 2+ items selected). Both buttons on the same line.
- Tapping a collapsed superset row selects all its member exercises.
- Tapping [Link]: all selected exercises merge into one superset group, capped at 5 exercises (6th selection is blocked with a toast). Non-adjacent selections are reordered to sit together at the position of the highest-ranked exercise in the selection. Edit mode exits and the list returns to 3-dot mode.
- Tapping [Cancel]: exits edit mode, nothing changes.

Unlinking supersets:
- 3-dot on a collapsed superset row → 'Unlink superset'. Atomic: dissolves the entire group, all exercises return to standalone rows at the position the superset occupied, in their previous internal order.
- No partial removal from a superset. To change membership: unlink all, re-link the desired subset.

Reordering within a superset:
- Cannot be done from the main template list (the superset is a single collapsed row).
- Internal order is managed on the superset's detail page, which has its own per-exercise drag handles.
- Dragging exercise A below exercise B within the detail page swaps their order but keeps both in the superset.

Exercise picker (adding exercises to a template):
- Search input (searches exercise name). Results sorted by last_used_at DESC so recently used exercises surface first.
- Two sections: 'My exercises' (user-created) and 'Exercise library' (global seed). Both searchable.
- Tap an exercise to add it to the bottom of the template list.
- '+' button to create a new exercise inline (name, muscle group, tracking type).

Template list (the /workouts/templates route):
- Sorted by last_used_at DESC.
- Each row: template name, exercise count, last used date (e.g. '3 days ago').
- Search input to filter by name.

UPDATE (2026-07-20) — follows the workouts-001 scoping decision:

Both 'sorted by last_used_at DESC' orderings are PER-USER AND DERIVED, not

- Template list: order by MAX(workout_sessions.started_at) for sessions where
  template_id = the template AND created_by_user_id = current user. A template
  someone else in the household used recently must NOT float to the top of your
  list. Templates you have never used sort last, not first.
- Exercise picker: order by the current user's most recent use, derived through
  session_exercises joined to workout_sessions filtered to that user.

Templates are household-shared, so the picker and list show every household
template regardless of who created it — only the ORDERING is personal.

features.title: Workout session logging UX — live logging, ghost values, rest timer, save-as-template prompt
features.description:
The active session experience: starting a workout, logging sets in real time, and wrapping up. Requires workouts-001 (data model) and workouts-002 (templates) to be complete first.

Starting a session:
- 'New workout' button on the workouts page. Options: pick a template (list sorted by last_used_at DESC, with search), or start blank.
- Starting from a template: session opens with all template exercises pre-loaded as session_exercises. Ghost values (muted, slightly transparent) pre-fill each set's weight and reps fields from the most recent session that used the same template_exercise_id. If no prior session exists for that template, fields are empty.
- Starting blank: empty session, user adds exercises via the same exercise picker as the template builder.

Session overview (the main list view):
- One row per exercise (standalone or collapsed superset, same visual rules as the template builder).
- Each row shows: exercise name, target sets from template (e.g. '3×8'), and a completion indicator (e.g. '✓ 2/3 sets').
- Tap anywhere on a row (except the 3-dot handle) to open the exercise detail page.
- A persistent header shows session duration (live timer) and a 'Finish workout' button.

Exercise detail page:
- Shows a table of sets: set number | [weight input] × [reps input] | ✓ button.
- Ghost values (muted style) pre-populate weight and reps from the previous session for the same exercise. Tapping any field activates it and clears the ghost state for that field.
- Warmup sets (is_warmup=true) are displayed in a smaller, muted style above the working sets with a 'W' badge. They do not count toward the completion indicator on the overview.
- A 'W+ Add warmup set' button above the working sets; '+ Add set' button at the bottom copies the last set's values as a starting point.
- Tapping ✓ on a set marks it complete (completed_at = now), triggers the rest timer, and advances the highlighted row to the next set.
- Rest timer: displayed at the bottom of the detail page. Starts automatically when a set is marked complete. Shows countdown from the template's default_rest_seconds (or a fallback of 90s). User can tap to dismiss or adjust. Timer persists if the user navigates back to the overview and returns.
- Optional rpe field per set (shown as a subtle 1–10 input below the reps field, collapsed by default; a 'Show RPE' toggle in session settings enables it).
- Target_reps field: shown as a muted reference next to the reps input if set (e.g. '— target: 8'). Reps logged vs. target_reps feeds into the progress chart failure detection.

Superset detail page:
- Shows both (or all) exercises in the group together, interleaved by round.
- ROUND 1: Exercise A sets, Exercise B sets. ROUND 2: same. Rest timer fires after completing one full round (after the last exercise in a round is checked off).
- '+ Add round' at the bottom adds a set to every exercise in the superset simultaneously.

Finishing a session:
- 'Finish workout' shows a summary: total duration, total working-set volume (weight × reps, warmup sets excluded), exercises completed.
- If prompt_save_as_template is true AND the session was NOT started from a template, a modal appears: 'Save this as a template?' with [Skip] and [Save Template] buttons, plus a 'Don't ask me again' checkbox. If the checkbox is checked on Skip, prompt_save_as_template is set to false. The option remains accessible as a secondary 'Save as template' button on the session summary screen regardless of this setting.
- Settings → Workouts contains a 'Prompt to save new workouts as templates' toggle that re-enables the prompt if turned off.

UPDATE (2026-07-20) — corrects a cross-user leak in the ghost-value rule:

Ghost values must filter to the CURRENT USER's sessions. As originally written
('the most recent session that used the same template_exercise_id') the query
has no user predicate, which breaks as soon as templates are shared per
workouts-001: a kid starting a session from a parent's template would be
pre-filled with the parent's weights. That is both a cross-user data leak and a
discouraging first experience.

Corrected rule: prefill from the most recent session where template_exercise_id
matches AND created_by_user_id = current user. If that user has never run this
template slot, fall back to the template's default_weight / default_reps, then
to empty. Never fall back to another member's data.

Keying on template_exercise_id (not exercise_id) is deliberate and worth
preserving: it means a heavy bench slot and a back-off bench slot in the same
template each track their own history, which is what makes progressive overload
prefill behave sensibly when protocols vary.

features.title: Workout progress tracking — per-exercise trends, estimated 1RM, volume charts
features.description:
A Progress tab on the workouts page showing how each exercise has changed over time. Requires workouts-001 (first-class sets) to be complete. Warmup sets (is_warmup=true) are excluded from all calculations.

Endpoint: GET /workouts/progress/:exercise_id?limit=20 returns a time-series of sessions: [{session_date, sets: [{reps, weight, is_warmup, target_reps}]}] for the given exercise, ordered oldest to newest, excluding warmup sets.

Frontend — Progress tab:
- Lists all exercises the user has logged in at least 2 sessions, sorted by most recently logged.
- Each row shows the exercise name and a sparkline (tiny inline trend of max weight over last 5 sessions).
- Tapping an exercise opens a full-screen progress detail view with:
  (1) Max weight chart: line chart of the heaviest working set per session over time.
  (2) Estimated 1RM chart: Epley formula applied per session — 1RM ≈ weight × (1 + reps / 30). Calculated client-side, never stored. Only shown for exercises with reps ≤ 10 (high-rep sets produce unreliable 1RM estimates).
  (3) Volume chart: total working volume per session (sum of weight × reps across all working sets).
  (4) A 'Failed sets' indicator: sessions where logged reps < target_reps on any working set are marked with a small ✗ on the timeline.
- Toggle between the three chart types via a segmented control at the top of the detail view.
- Bodyweight exercises (weight=null): only the reps chart is shown (max reps per session, volume as total reps).

UPDATE (2026-07-20) — follows the workouts-001 scoping decision:

GET /workouts/progress/:exercise_id returns ONLY the requesting user's sessions.
Progress history is personal even though the exercise catalog is shared —
household members must never appear in each other's charts, and the endpoint
must filter created_by_user_id server-side rather than relying on the client.
The 'exercises logged in at least 2 sessions' list is likewise per-user.

features.title: Legacy workout model cutover — retire Workout/ExerciseEntry for one session-based representation
features.description:
workouts-001 (migration 0048) added the session/exercise/set model and backfilled the legacy workouts/exercise_entries tables into it, but left the legacy tables live and writable behind the old /workouts endpoints — two writable representations of the same data. This retires the legacy model entirely so there is one representation.

Before dropping it runs a safety-net backfill for any legacy workout 0048 never migrated: 0048's backfill SKIPS entirely if any workout_sessions row already exists, so on a DB where a session was created through the new API before 0048 ran, the legacy rows were never copied. 0049 keys correspondence on (household_id, created_by_user_id, created_at) — 0048 copied the legacy created_at onto its session — to migrate only the un-migrated rows with no false positives, then drops. downgrade recreates the table structure but cannot restore rows (documented as forward-only for data). Existence-guarded so it is a no-op where the tables are already absent.

- Migrated web/workouts/page.tsx onto /workouts/sessions + /workouts/exercises (no compatibility adapter); regenerated schema.d.ts; updated the realtime invalidation map for the new tables.
- Repointed the ai/tools.py coach workout tools (create/list/get/update/delete) onto the session model, translating aggregate metrics into first-class sets and resolving exercise names against the catalog. MCP tools already pointed at the new model.

features.title: Run Alembic migrations on SQLite — stamp-at-head, forward-only
features.description: ADR: plans/014-sqlite-schema-evolution.md (decision B2). Today SQLite installs never run Alembic — migrations/env.py:80 hard-returns on a SQLite URL, and schema comes from create_all() plus _patch_sqlite_schema(), which silently SKIPS unique constraints, adds NOT NULL columns as nullable, and never runs data backfills. Fresh Tauri installs are mostly correct (create_all builds current ORM metadata); UPDATED installs silently diverge — and that is the trial-to-paid population. Already bit twice: collection.kind (migration 0032's Postgres-only backfill, hand-patched via backfill_journal_kind) and plan 011's unique index (plans/README.md:31). Fix: remove the SQLite early-return in env.py, set render_as_batch=_is_sqlite() in do_run_migrations, run `alembic stamp head` after create_all_tables() on a fresh SQLite DB, and DELETE _patch_sqlite_schema() and its call site — it is the drift generator. Historical migrations 0001-0045 never replay on SQLite and need no audit; production Postgres is untouched (railway.json runs `alembic upgrade head` on deploy). Also correct the obsolete pgloader advice in the env.py SQLite message. Going forward every migration must be SQLite-safe: batch mode covers most ALTER limits, but raw op.execute with Postgres-specific SQL needs a dialect guard — document this in api/CLAUDE.md alongside the idempotency rules.

It does two jobs: tag existing kind=NULL notes collections that look like journals, and seed a journal collection for households lacking one. Both jobs are therefore purely historical and belong in a migration. Folding also removes a per-boot scan of every household with a query each — an N+1 that is trivial on single-household desktop and real on multi-household cloud. The only capability lost is self-healing against a future code path that creates a household without seeding; that is speculative, and better guarded by a test or DB constraint than a permanent boot scan.

features.title: Agent proposals — propose permission tier, model, and audit double-attribution
features.description: Design: plans/open-hearth/agent-proposals.md (track 7 of plans/open-hearth.md). Adds a third permission tier ordered read < propose < write, so an agent write that today either executes or 403s gains a middle outcome: it is captured as a pending Proposal for a human to approve or reject. Two layers gain the value. Token scopes: {"todos": "propose"} becomes legal; effective permission = min(token, ceiling) under the new ordering. Member ceilings: permissions_config actions gain propose as an assignable rank outcome, backward compatible — no existing config resolves to propose unless explicitly set. mcp/auth.py:authorize() currently returns PatIdentity or raises; it must instead return a decision carrying the resolved tier, since propose is neither success nor failure. Write tools change in exactly one way: when authorize resolves to propose, the tool records a Proposal instead of executing and returns {"status": "proposed", "proposal_id": ..., "message": ...} — the message is part of the tool contract so agents relay it naturally rather than reporting an error. New proposals table is surface-agnostic from day one (DECIDED 2026-07-20): proposed_by_user_id nullable (household-agent), token_id nullable (web-UI proposals have no token), source column reusing the existing AuditSource vocabulary (web|mcp|script — NOT a new agent|web one; audit_log.source already uses these and two divergent 'source' vocabularies is a trap), so proposal-003 adds the web path with no migration. CRITICAL: proposals.token_id must NOT be ON DELETE SET NULL, unlike audit_log.token_id. The stale-proposer guard has to distinguish a legitimately-null household-agent token_id from a token revoked after proposing; under SET NULL those states are identical and the guard fails open. This is also why proposals cannot reuse audit_log despite sharing ~9 columns: audit_log is append-only by design (proposals mutate through pending -> approved/rejected/expired), its payload is contractually a lossy summary while args must be the exact replayable service call, and the two have opposite retention (audit is permanent history, proposals expire and are swept). Note the propose TIER itself needs no DDL — scopes and permissions_config are both JSON columns — so this migration is exactly one new table. Proposals are idempotent like every other write — identical pending args return the same proposal rather than duplicating. Approval executes the original write through the same service function and records TWO audit facts: proposed_by (agent/token) and approved_by (human). Approval re-validates against the APPROVER's ceiling, requiring write on the domain (DECIDED 2026-07-20 — approval is the approver's act; the proposer's ceiling already did its job by routing to propose). One guard on audit-integrity grounds: approval refuses proposals whose token was revoked or whose proposer left the household, since executing those attributes a write to a credential that no longer exists. Expiry sweep (default 7 days) piggybacks on the existing APScheduler jobs. MIGRATION: yes — serialize with other migration-bearing builds per root CLAUDE.md; verify a single alembic head after rebase. This build is the model and semantics only; the approval queue UI, notifications, and MCP status tools are proposal-002.

SCOPE TEST: token with write on todos calls add_todo and verify it executes immediately — the propose tier must not intercept a genuine write

features.title: Agent proposals — approval queue UI, realtime notification, and MCP status tools
features.description: Design: plans/open-hearth/agent-proposals.md. Second half of the proposals track; depends on proposal-001 (model + semantics). Surfaces the pending queue to the humans who decide it and closes the loop back to the agent that proposed. APPROVAL QUEUE: a /proposals page plus a dashboard widget, each row showing the summary string, who proposed it (member or named device on the household-agent token), the domain, and approve / reject-with-reason actions. REALTIME + NOTIFICATION: bus events proposal.created and proposal.decided on the existing event bus (realtime-001); SSE already delivers them, so the queue updates live. Routing is ALL ADMINS, configurable later (DECIDED 2026-07-20) — every owner/admin sees the queue, first-to-decide wins, and an admin opening an already-decided proposal sees the decision and who made it rather than a stale approve button. No routing config in the schema yet; per-domain approver routing is the natural v2 and lands in permissions_config when asked for. MCP TOOLS: list_my_proposals and get_proposal_status let an agent see what it has pending and why something was rejected, so it can tell its user rather than going silent. Approving stays human/UI-only in v1 — an agent approving proposals defeats the point. Per the root CLAUDE.md parity principle, these tool descriptions and the proposed-status messages are agent UX and are written to the same bar as UI copy: enumerate valid values, suggest the alternative on a miss, and never surface a bare error code. VOICE RENDERING: the voice bridge renders status=proposed playfully ("I'll ask your parents") rather than reading a status string. Bridge-layer and optional. HARD RULE from the design doc: approving happens only on authenticated surfaces (app/push), never on a voice device — device identity proves where a request came from, never who spoke.

features.title: Outbound webhooks — semantic event layer + subscriptions + signed delivery worker
features.description:
Design: plans/open-hearth/outbound-webhooks.md (track 7 of plans/open-hearth.md). Makes Hearth an event SOURCE, the mirror of HA inbound. Migration-bearing — serialize against proposal-001.

PREREQUISITE DISCOVERED 2026-07-20: the track doc's original event catalog was fiction. events/emit.py is a universal TABLE-LEVEL invalidation producer (after_flush/after_commit listeners emitting InvalidationEvent(entity_type=<tablename>, action=created|updated|deleted)); there are zero bus.publish/emit calls under domains/. So todo.completed did not exist (a completion is todos+updated, indistinguishable from a title edit), and grocery.item_added / grocery.item_checked / habit.checked_in COULD NOT emit at all because grocery_items and habit_occurrences carry no household_id. This feature therefore builds the semantic event layer first.

SEMANTIC LAYER (decided 2026-07-20): the universal producer is left untouched (it feeds SSE invalidation; changing it breaks live UI). Semantic events ride the SAME commit-time plumbing — domain service functions append a SemanticEvent to session.info under its own key, mirroring _PENDING_KEY, and the existing after_commit listener publishes them alongside the invalidations. This inherits the proven guarantees for free: nothing emits for a transaction that rolls back, and a publish failure never breaks the committed write. Child tables become emittable because the service function knows the parent and emits explicitly with the parent's household_id and the parent's visibility descriptor — the follow-up anticipated by emit.py's own coverage-caveat docstring. events/scope.py REMAINS THE SINGLE SCOPE MECHANISM: can_see is widened from InvalidationEvent to the descriptor fields (visibility, created_by_user_id, shared_with_user_ids) so both event kinds pass through one unchanged function. Do not invent a second filter.

CATALOG v1: todo.created, todo.completed, grocery.item_added, grocery.item_checked, habit.checked_in, calendar.event_created. Child events inherit the parent's visibility. proposal.* is deliberately excluded — proposal-001 has not landed; it is the first addition once it does.

SUBSCRIPTIONS: new webhook_subscriptions table (id, household_id, created_by, url, secret encrypted via FIELD_ENCRYPTION_KEY — it is needed for signing so it cannot be hashed, event_patterns JSONB, active, consecutive_failures, last_delivery_at, created_at). Member-owned: a subscription delivers only events its OWNER is entitled to see under can_see, so a household-agent-owned subscription receives shared-scope events only. Note: there is no 'sensitive' visibility in the code — core/visibility.py has household|personal|members — so the operative rule is that a personal or members event is never delivered to a subscription whose owner fails can_see.

PAYLOAD: skinny, like SSE — {event, entity_type, entity_id, household_id, occurred_at, summary}. Receivers wanting more fetch back through REST with their own credentials, keeping scope enforcement in one place. DECIDED 2026-07-20: the per-event field allowlist lives in ONE central module (webhooks/summaries.py) mapping event name -> permitted field names, and the delivery worker filters every summary through it before signing. Leak review is then a single-file read, and a domain cannot accidentally widen the payload.

DELIVERY: async worker consuming the bus, durable queue table webhook_deliveries giving at-least-once with a delivery id for receiver dedupe. Signature X-Hearth-Signature: t=<unix>, v1=HMAC-SHA256(secret, t + '.' + body), timestamped to block replay; receiver verification documented in the API docs. Retries on exponential backoff (30s/5m/30m/2h/6h) then mark failed; auto-disable the subscription after N consecutive failures (Stripe-style) and surface that in the UI. Timeout ~5s, response body ignored, 2xx = delivered.

DELIVERY LOG (decided 2026-07-20): attempts and retry state live ONLY in webhook_deliveries (high volume, prunable). Subscription LIFECYCLE events — created, paused, deleted, auto-disabled — write one audit_log row each, because those are human-initiated decisions about where household data may egress. Do not write an audit_log row per delivery attempt; audit_log is indexed (household_id, created_at) for a human-readable Activity page and would be flooded.

FILTERS (decided 2026-07-20): event_patterns is the ENTIRE filter surface in v1. No assignee/parent filters — that is a webhook-002 extension if demand appears. Any future filter must apply strictly AFTER can_see: a filter narrows, it can never widen.

SSRF GUARD: tier-dependent via the existing DEPLOYMENT_TIER. Cloud tier rejects private/loopback/link-local ranges and re-resolves DNS at delivery time (guarding DNS rebinding); self-hosted permits LAN targets because pointing at your own HA box is the entire point.

MCP PARITY: satisfied by the bus event itself — root CLAUDE.md accepts 'a tool, resource, or bus event as appropriate', and the outbound event IS the agent-facing surface here. The management TOOLS (list_webhooks / create_webhook) are webhook-002.

UI: Settings -> Integrations -> Webhooks (create/list/pause/delete, secret shown once). Docs: an HA recipe showing a normal subscription pointed at /api/webhook/<id> plus sample automation YAML consuming trigger.json — note HA cannot verify the HMAC, so that path relies on webhook-ID secrecy plus the LAN boundary.

REPLAY: replay a captured delivery with a stale t and verify the documented receiver-side timestamp check rejects it

SCOPE LEAK (critical): member A creates a PERSONAL todo; member B owns a subscription matching todo.created — verify B's endpoint receives NOTHING. Repeat for a members-visibility entity where B is not in shared_with_user_ids
SCOPE PARITY: verify the delivery filter calls events/scope.py can_see and that no second filtering path exists (grep for a duplicate visibility check)

features.title: Outbound webhooks — MCP management tools, delivery log UI, HA preset
features.description:
Design: plans/open-hearth/outbound-webhooks.md. Follow-on to webhook-001; no migration expected beyond an optional filters column if per-subscription filters are taken up.

MCP MANAGEMENT TOOLS: list_webhooks / create_webhook, write-scoped, so an agent can wire ITSELF up. The flagship demo is an agent subscribing itself to grocery.item_added and reacting. Tool descriptions are agent UX per root CLAUDE.md — enumerate the valid event names from the v1 catalog and, on an unknown pattern, name the problem and list what is available rather than returning a bare error.

DELIVERY LOG UI: last N attempts per subscription with status, response code, attempt count, and next retry time; surface the auto-disabled state prominently with a re-enable action.

HA PRESET (decided 2026-07-20): a UI prefill only — it fills the /api/webhook/<id> URL shape and links the recipe docs shipped in webhook-001. Explicitly NOT an HA-shaped payload variant: a second payload shape would break the one-contract property the skinny design buys and would force the allowlist to be enforced twice.

DEFERRED FROM v1, build here only if demand appears: per-subscription filters beyond event_patterns (e.g. only todos assigned to member X), as a fixed enumerated set on a JSONB filters column, applied strictly AFTER can_see. Motivation if it comes up: because payloads are skinny, a receiver cannot filter locally on a field it was never sent, so narrowing otherwise costs an authenticated REST round-trip per event.

features.title: Reconcile native Postgres enums with the ORM models
features.description: Design: plans/015-enum-drift-reconciliation.md (ADR-015). Migration 0047 converts the seven native Postgres enum columns (collections.domain, documents.kind, exercise_entries.type, goals.priority, todos.priority, household_memberships.role, projects.status) to VARCHAR + CHECK, then drops the six types plus two orphans (note_kind, actor_type). The models already declared native_enum=False but emitted NO constraint, because create_constraint has defaulted to False since SQLAlchemy 1.4 — so each declaration gained name= and create_constraint=True, making create_all and the migration produce identical DDL. Closes the failure class behind the 0046 Railway pre-deploy crash, where a VARCHAR-bound param was compared against a native enum column ('operator does not exist: collection_domain = character varying'). priority_level backs two columns, so types drop only after every column converts. On SQLite there is no type to convert, but the CHECKs are still added via batch_alter_table so a database created before this revision matches one created after.

pg_constraint shows all 7 CHECKs with the enum type names (priority_level twice)

SQLite: upgrade keeps every row through the table rebuild, CHECK rejects an invalid value, downgrade drops the CHECKs and keeps data
